new_note: *Those are the ten tribes, which were carried away prisoners out of their own land in the time of Osea the king, whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria led away captive, and he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land.* (2 Esdras 13:40). *But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 10:6). Ezra is told plainly who the peaceable multitude of his vision is: the ten tribes Shalmaneser carried out of their own land and over the waters, who never came back. Those are the people the King means when he sends the twelve to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel). A sheep is lost when it has wandered where the shepherd cannot see it, and the northern house had been lost in another land for seven centuries by the time Yahusha (Jesus) spoke these words. The mission of the twelve was aimed at the same body Ezra was shown.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:40 — *Those are the ten tribes, which were carried away prisoners out of their own land.* The lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel) the twelve are sent to at Matthew 10:6.

new_note: *Those are the ten tribes, which were carried away prisoners out of their own land in the time of Osea the king, whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria led away captive, and he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land.* (2 Esdras 13:40). *But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 15:24). When the woman of Canaan pressed him, Yahusha (Jesus) named the scope of his sending: the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel) — and she, who heard the Shepherd and would not be turned away, was one of them. Ezra had already been shown who that house is, the ten tribes Shalmaneser led away captive over the waters into another land, who never returned. The lost sheep were not a figure of speech; they were a people with a date, a captor, and a direction of travel, the same carrying away the book of Kings records (2 Kings 17:6). The King was sent to them, and the prophets who promised their gathering (Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 37) were speaking of the same people.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:40 — *whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria led away captive.* The lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel) the King says he was sent to (Matthew 15:24).

new_note: *Those are the ten tribes, which were carried away prisoners out of their own land in the time of Osea the king, whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria led away captive, and he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land.* (2 Esdras 13:40). *Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit):* (Matthew 28:19). Set these two side by side and the Great Commission stops reading as a change of audience. Ezra was shown the ten tribes carried over the waters into another land, and that land is among the nations; the scattered house lives there, mixed in and unrecognizable, the people Hosea called not my people (Hosea 1:9). So the King who said he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel) now sends his disciples to all nations, because that is where the sheep are. The scope widened to every nation because the flock is scattered through every nation, not because the flock was replaced. We do not know those sheep by sight, so the word goes out broadly, and the ones who hear are revealed to be his (John 10:27).
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:40 — *he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land.* The scattered house lives among the nations, which is why the word goes to all nations (Matthew 28:19).

new_note: *Those are the ten tribes, which were carried away prisoners out of their own land in the time of Osea the king, whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria led away captive, and he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land.* (2 Esdras 13:40). *And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost.* (Luke 15:6). The sheep in the parable was lost, and the shepherd went after it until he found it, then called his neighbours to rejoice. Ezra was told who the lost are: the ten tribes carried over the waters into another land, where they dwelt until the latter time, *and now when they shall begin to come* (2 Esdras 13:46). The joy Yahusha (Jesus) describes is the joy of that homecoming. A lost sheep is still the shepherd's sheep the whole time it is lost; the ten tribes were still the house of Yashar'el (Israel) in the far country, and the finding is the gathering the prophets promised.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:40 — *carried away prisoners out of their own land.* The lost sheep whose finding the shepherd rejoices over at Luke 15:6.

new_note: *But they took this counsel among themselves, that they would leave the multitude of the heathen, and go forth into a further country, where never mankind dwelt, That they might there keep their statutes, which they never kept in their own land.* (2 Esdras 13:41–42). *But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 10:6). The tribes did not simply vanish into the heathen. Ezra is told they took counsel to leave the multitude and go further out, into a country where no one lived, so that they could keep the statutes they had never kept in their own land. The carrying away became, for a remnant of them, a going out to keep Torah. Centuries later the King sends the twelve to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel), the same body, in the lands it went out to. The commandments they carried into the far country are what the sheep are being called back to, and Yahusha (Jesus) sends his messengers after them rather than waiting for them to find the way home alone.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:41 — *they would leave the multitude of the heathen, and go forth into a further country.* The remnant went out to keep the statutes; the twelve are sent after them (Matthew 10:6).
flag: Old note quoted 13:41-42 together and its point (keeping the statutes) sits in v.42, so both verses are quoted and cited as 13:41-42.

new_note: *The Highest shall stay the springs of the stream again, that they may go through: therefore sawest you the multitude with peace.* (2 Esdras 13:47). *But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Yashar'el (Israel), till the Son of Adam be come.* (Matthew 10:23). The Most High stayed the river once so the tribes could cross out, and Ezra is promised he will stay it again so they can cross back, in the latter time. That return is the end of the story the vision tells. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the twelve they will not finish going over the cities of Yashar'el (Israel) before the Son of Adam comes; the work he sends them on is not completed in their lifetime but runs until his coming. Set together, the two say the same thing: the going after the lost sheep and the gathering of the ten tribes are one work, begun with the sending and finished when the Highest opens the way home and the King returns.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:47 — *The Highest shall stay the springs of the stream again, that they may go through.* The way home opens at the latter time; the mission runs till the Son of Adam comes (Matthew 10:23).

new_note: *The Highest shall stay the springs of the stream again, that they may go through: therefore sawest you the multitude with peace.* (2 Esdras 13:47). *Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit):* (Matthew 28:19). Ezra sees the ten tribes come back through the stream the Most High stays for them; the peaceable multitude of his vision is the scattered house coming home, and it is the Highest who does the gathering. Yahusha (Jesus) sends his disciples to all nations, and these two verses explain each other: the disciples go out into the nations because that is where the tribes were carried, and the Father brings them back. Isaiah had already said he would set his hand the second time to recover the remnant of his people from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:11–12); James wrote to the twelve tribes scattered abroad (James 1:1), and Peter to the strangers scattered through the provinces (1 Peter 1:1). The proclamation to all nations is that second recovery going out to find them.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:47 — *stay the springs of the stream again, that they may go through.* The Father brings the tribes back; the disciples go to all nations because that is where they were carried (Matthew 28:19).

new_note: *The Highest shall stay the springs of the stream again, that they may go through: therefore sawest you the multitude with peace.* (2 Esdras 13:47). *And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven.* (Mark 13:27). The ten tribes did not find their own way home in Ezra's vision. The Highest stayed the springs of the stream for them, as he had once held the waters when they went out, and the multitude came through in peace. Mark 13:27 is the same homecoming seen from the gospel side: when the Son of Adam comes, he sends his angels to gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of the earth to the other. The gathering is his act in both books. The scattered seed is brought back by the hand of the Most High, not by its own contriving, and the elect of Mark 13 are the people Ezra watched cross the stream.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:47 — *therefore sawest you the multitude with peace.* The act of the Most High, not the scattered's own contriving; Mark 13:27's elect gathered from the four winds.

new_note: *But those that be left behind of your people are they that are found within my borders.* (2 Esdras 13:48). *But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel).* (Matthew 15:24). The vision does not forget the ones who never left. After the ten tribes come home, Ezra is told that those left behind of his people are the ones found within the borders of the land, the remnant of Yahudah (Judah) that stayed. When Yahusha (Jesus) says he was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Yashar'el (Israel), his sending reaches both of these: the multitudes of Galilee and Yahudah (Judah) he walked among inside the borders, and the scattered house beyond the waters his apostles would be sent after. The house of Yashar'el (Israel) is both of them, the ones who stayed and the ones who were carried, and the King's mission is to the whole house.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:48 — *those that be left behind of your people are they that are found within my borders.* The remnant that stayed; the King's mission reaches them and the scattered alike (Matthew 15:24).

new_note: *Then the high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children:* (2 Maccabees 3:10). *Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child.* (Exodus 22:22). Heliodorus came to Jerusalem to take the temple treasury for the king, and the high priest told him what the money was: provision laid up for widows and the fatherless. The Torah had already spoken over that money. Yahuah (God) commanded that no widow or fatherless child be afflicted, and the verses that follow promise that his wrath will wax hot against any who do it (Exodus 22:23–24). What looked to Heliodorus like a king's revenue was the very thing the Torah guards, and the rest of the chapter shows the guard was real.
member_note: 2 Maccabees 3:10 — *such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children.* The treasury Heliodorus came for was the Torah's protected ones (Exodus 22:22).

new_note: *For there appeared to them an horse with a terrible rider upon him, and adorned with a very fair covering, and he ran fiercely, and struck at Heliodorus with his forefeet, and it seemed that he that sat upon the horse had complete harness of gold.* (2 Maccabees 3:25). *And it came to pass, when Joshua was by Jericho, that he lifted up his eyes and looked, and, behold, there stood a man over against him with his sword drawn in his hand: and Joshua went unto him, and said unto him, Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?* (Joshua 5:13). When Heliodorus pressed into the treasury, a rider in golden harness appeared and struck at him, and all who came in with him were astonished at the power of Yahuah (God). Joshua met the same kind of presence by Jericho: a man standing with his sword drawn, who named himself captain of the host of Yahuah (LORD) and told Joshua the ground he stood on was holy (Joshua 5:14–15). In both places an armed one stands up for the place and the people of Yahuah (God) when a stranger comes against them. The captain who stood for Jericho stood again in the treasury, and the defense of the temple was not left to men.
member_note: 2 Maccabees 3:25 — *an horse with a terrible rider upon him, and adorned with a very fair covering.* The armed one standing for the place of Yahuah (God), as the captain stood by Jericho (Joshua 5:13).

new_note: *Promising to the king by intercession three hundred and threescore talents of silver, and of another revenue eighty talents:* (2 Maccabees 4:8). *The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon Yahuah (LORD), and say, Is not Yahuah (LORD) among us? none evil can come upon us.* (Micah 3:11). Jason did not inherit the high priesthood; he bought it. He went to Antiochus behind his brother Onias and promised three hundred and sixty talents of silver, with eighty more from another revenue, to be made high priest. Micah had already named that transaction: heads who judge for reward, priests who teach for hire, prophets who divine for money, all of them still saying Yahuah (LORD) is among us and no evil can come. The office was turned into a purchase, and the chapters that follow show how much evil did come. A priesthood bought for silver is the thing the prophet condemned, in whatever age it appears.
member_note: 2 Maccabees 4:8 — *Promising to the king by intercession three hundred and threescore talents of silver.* The priesthood bought for silver; priests that teach for hire (Micah 3:11).

new_note: *That the priests had no courage to serve any more at the altar, but despising the temple, and neglecting the sacrifices, hastened to be partakers of the unlawful allowance in the place of exercise, after the game of Discus called them forth;* (2 Maccabees 4:14). *But ye are departed out of the way; ye have caused many to stumble at the law; ye have corrupted the covenant of Levi, saith Yahuah Tseva'ot (LORD of hosts).* (Malachi 2:8). Under Jason the priests lost their stomach for the altar. They despised the temple, neglected the sacrifices, and ran to the Greek gymnasium when the discus called, taking their share of what the Torah forbade. Malachi had already said what that is: priests departed out of the way, causing many to stumble at the law, corrupting the covenant of Levi. The threat to the temple in these chapters did not begin with Antiochus; it began at the altar, with the men set apart to serve there. The covenant of Levi was broken from the inside before any king broke in.
member_note: 2 Maccabees 4:14 — *the priests had no courage to serve any more at the altar, but despising the temple.* The covenant of Levi corrupted from within (Malachi 2:8).

new_note: *And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You like a fury takest us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise us up, who have died for his laws, to everlasting life.* (2 Maccabees 7:9). *Yahusha (Jesus) answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of Elohim (God).* (Matthew 22:29). The second of the seven brothers, dying under Antiochus for refusing to break the Torah, said with his last breath that the King of the world would raise him up to everlasting life. He did not hold a philosophy about the afterlife; he held a hope in the resurrection, and he paid for it with his body. When the Sadducees, who said there is no resurrection (Acts 23:8), came to trap Yahusha (Jesus), he told them they erred because they knew neither the scriptures nor the power of Elohim (God). The brothers in 2 Maccabees 7 knew both. The resurrection the King defended in the temple was the resurrection a family had already confessed under torture, for his laws.
member_note: 2 Maccabees 7:9 — *the King of the world shall raise us up, who have died for his laws, to everlasting life.* The resurrection confessed in blood; the Sadducees erred, not knowing the power of Elohim (God) (Matthew 22:29).

new_note: *But doubtless the Creator of the world, who formed the generation of man, and found out the beginning of all things, will also of his own mercy give you breath and life again, as you now regard not your own selves for his laws’ sake.* (2 Maccabees 7:23). *I am the Elohim (God) of Abraham, and the Elohim (God) of Isaac, and the Elohim (God) of Jacob? Elohim (God) is not the Elohim (God) of the dead, but of the living.* (Matthew 22:32). The mother tells her sons where life comes from: she did not give them breath, the Creator did, and the one who formed man at the beginning can give breath and life again. That is her whole comfort as they die. Yahusha (Jesus) makes the same argument from the same ground: Elohim (God) names himself the Elohim (God) of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and he is not the Elohim (God) of the dead but of the living, so the fathers must rise. Neither the mother nor the King speaks of souls already in heaven; both look to the Creator giving breath again to those who sleep. The seven sons and their mother lie down in that hope, waiting with the fathers for the day their breath is given back.
member_note: 2 Maccabees 7:23 — *will also of his own mercy give you breath and life again.* The Creator gives breath again; Elohim (God) of the living, not of the dead (Matthew 22:32).

new_note: *For our brothers, who now have suffered a short pain, are dead under the covenant of Yahuah (God) of everlasting life: but you, through the judgment of Yahuah (God), shall receive just punishment for your pride.* (2 Maccabees 7:36). *For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.* (Matthew 26:28). The youngest brother says his brothers are dead under the covenant of Yahuah (God) of everlasting life. They died for his laws, and their deaths are held inside a covenant that promises them life again. At the last supper Yahusha (Jesus) names his blood as the blood of the new covenant, shed for many for the remission of sins. The covenant the martyrs died under and the covenant the King's blood seals are not two covenants; the brothers trusted a promise of everlasting life, and the King's death and third-day rising are where that promise was made good. Their short pain and his cup end in the same resurrection, and the Torah they died for is the Torah the new covenant writes on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33).
member_note: 2 Maccabees 7:36 — *are dead under the covenant of Yahuah (God) of everlasting life.* The covenant the martyrs died under is sealed in the King's blood (Matthew 26:28).
flag: Old note ran off into a Reformation/eternal-security digression (Romans 6:14-15, Deuteronomy 28) beyond what these two verses carry; kept only the covenant-of-everlasting-life connection and the Torah-on-the-heart line.

new_note: *For our brothers, who now have suffered a short pain, are dead under the covenant of Yahuah (God) of everlasting life: but you, through the judgment of Yahuah (God), shall receive just punishment for your pride.* (2 Maccabees 7:36). *And he said unto them, This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many.* (Mark 14:24). Dying under Antiochus, the youngest brother names where his brothers now lie: dead under the covenant of Yahuah (God) of everlasting life. They were faithful to the covenant unto death, and the covenant holds them. At the table Yahusha (Jesus) lifts the cup and calls it his blood of the new covenant, shed for many. The martyrs of 2 Maccabees 7 died trusting a covenant of everlasting life whose promise had not yet been made good; Mark 14:24 is the King's own blood put to that same covenant. The many it is shed for include the seven who went before it, and their everlasting life waits on the resurrection the King's own rising opened.
member_note: 2 Maccabees 7:36 — *are dead under the covenant of Yahuah (God) of everlasting life.* Mark 14:24's blood of the new covenant seals the covenant of everlasting life the martyrs died under.

new_note: *But I, as my brothers, offer up my body and life for the laws of our fathers, beseeching Yahuah (God) that he would speedily be merciful to our nation; and that you by torments and plagues may confess, that he alone is Yahuah (God);* (2 Maccabees 7:37). *But Yahusha (Jesus) answered and said, Ye know not what ye ask. Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of, and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with? They say unto him, We are able.* (Matthew 20:22). The youngest brother offers his body and life for the laws of his fathers and prays that in him and his brothers the wrath on the nation would cease (2 Maccabees 7:38). When James and John ask for the chief seats, Yahusha (Jesus) asks whether they can drink the cup he is about to drink, and they say they are able. The brothers under Antiochus had drunk a cup like that, giving their lives for the Torah and for mercy on their people. Only the King's cup carries the remission of sins; his death is the one no martyr could die. But the cost of following him is real, and the seven brothers show what the sons of Zebedee were agreeing to, James by the sword (Acts 12:2) and John in exile on Patmos (Revelation 1:9).
member_note: 2 Maccabees 7:37 — *offer up my body and life for the laws of our fathers.* The cup the sons of Zebedee said they could drink (Matthew 20:22).

new_note: *And having cleansed the temple they made another altar, and striking stones they took fire out of them, and offered a sacrifice after two years, and set forth incense, and lights, and shewbread.* (2 Maccabees 10:3). *And Yahusha (Jesus) went into the temple of Elohim (God), and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves,* (Matthew 21:12). Judas and his men cleansed what Antiochus had defiled: they pulled down the heathen altars, built a new altar, struck fresh fire from stones, and brought back the sacrifice, the incense, the lamps, and the shewbread after two years without them. Yahusha (Jesus) also walked into the temple and cleansed it, but the defilement he drove out had not come from a foreign king. It came from the house's own leadership, who had let the courts become a market, and he answered them with Jeremiah's words: *My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves* (Matthew 21:13; Jeremiah 7:11). The Maccabees cleansed the temple of a defilement pressed on it from outside; the King cleansed it of the one that grew up inside, in the very priesthood their victory had restored. Both cleansings say the same thing about whose house it is.
member_note: 2 Maccabees 10:3 — *having cleansed the temple they made another altar.* The temple cleansed of a defilement from outside; the King cleansed it from inside (Matthew 21:12).

new_note: *Therefore they bare branches, and fair boughs, and palms also, and sang psalms to him that had given them good success in cleansing his place.* (2 Maccabees 10:7). *And a very great multitude spread their garments in the way; others cut down branches from the trees, and strawed them in the way.* (Matthew 21:8). When the temple was cleansed, the people carried branches and fair boughs and palms and sang psalms to the one who had given them success in cleansing his place, keeping eight days with gladness like the feast of tabernacles (2 Maccabees 10:6). When Yahusha (Jesus) rode into Jerusalem, the multitude cut down branches and strewed them in the way and cried Hosanna from Psalm 118, and the next thing he did was walk into the temple and cleanse it. Branches, psalms, and a cleansed temple belong together in both books. The people at the gate were doing what their fathers had done after Judas's victory, whether they knew it or not, and the King they welcomed went straight to his Father's house as the Maccabees had gone to theirs.
member_note: 2 Maccabees 10:7 — *they bare branches, and fair boughs, and palms also, and sang psalms.* Branches and psalms before a cleansed temple, as at the entry (Matthew 21:8).

new_note: *Nevertheless upon the fifth day early twenty young men of Maccabeus’ company, inflamed with anger because of the blasphemies, assaulted the wall manly, and with a fierce courage killed all that they met withal.* (2 Maccabees 10:35). *Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, hath turned my wrath away from the children of Yashar'el (Israel), while he was zealous for my sake among them, that I consumed not the children of Yashar'el (Israel) in my jealousy.* (Numbers 25:11). The men inside the city trusted their walls and blasphemed from them, and on the fifth day twenty of Judas's young men, inflamed by the blasphemies, went up the wall. The book names the cause of their anger: not the siege, not the plunder, but the blasphemies. That is the zeal of Phinehas. Yahuah (God) said Phinehas turned his wrath away from Yashar'el (Israel) because he was zealous for his sake, and for that zeal gave him a covenant of peace (Numbers 25:12–13). Zeal for the name of Yahuah (God) when his name is mocked is the thread that runs from Phinehas's javelin to Judas's twenty.
member_note: 2 Maccabees 10:35 — *inflamed with anger because of the blasphemies.* The zeal of Phinehas for the name of Yahuah (God) (Numbers 25:11).

new_note: *And when they told him that this was not permissible, none of the nation, no, nor even the priests in general, but only the supreme high priest of all, and he only once in a year, being allowed to go in, he would by no means give way.* (3 Maccabees 1:11). *Therefore thou and thy sons with thee shall keep your priest’s office for every thing of the altar, and within the vail; and ye shall serve: I have given your priest’s office unto you as a service of gift: and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death.* (Numbers 18:7). Ptolemy saw the temple, admired it, and decided he would walk into the sanctuary itself. The priests told him the rule: no one of the nation, not even the priests, only the high priest, and he only once a year. The king called that an honour he was being denied; the Torah calls it a death sentence for anyone else who comes near. Yahuah (God) gave the priesthood to Aaron and his sons as a gift, within the vail as well as at the altar, and said the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death. The high priest's one entry a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2) was not a privilege to be extended; it was the boundary Yahuah (God) set on his own dwelling, and Ptolemy was pressing against the boundary and its penalty.
member_note: 3 Maccabees 1:11 — *only the supreme high priest of all, and he only once in a year.* The boundary of Numbers 18:7: the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death.

new_note: *And they said, Behold, we have sent you money to buy you burnt offerings, and sin offerings, and incense, and prepare you manna, and offer upon the altar of Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God); And pray for the life of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and for the life of Balthasar his son, that their days may be upon earth as the days of heaven:* (Baruch 1:10–11). *That they may offer sacrifices of sweet savours unto the Elohim (God) of heaven, and pray for the life of the king, and of his sons.* (Ezra 6:10). The exiles in Babylon sent silver back to Jerusalem for burnt offerings and sin offerings and incense, and in the same breath asked that prayer be made for the life of Nebuchadnezzar and his son. Darius's decree in Ezra does the same two things together: it provides for the sacrifices to the Elohim (God) of heaven and asks that the priests pray for the life of the king and his sons. Offering and prayer for the ruler go together in both, under a Babylonian king and under a Persian one. Jeremiah had told the captives to seek the peace of the city they were carried to and to pray for it (Jeremiah 29:7), and here are the captives doing exactly that, with the altar at the center of it.
member_note: Baruch 1:10 — *we have sent you money to buy you burnt offerings, and sin offerings, and incense.* Offerings and prayer for the king together, as in Darius's decree (Ezra 6:10).
flag: Old note's point (prayer for Nebuchadnezzar) sits in v.11, so 1:10-11 are quoted together and cited as Baruch 1:10-11.

new_note: *Who has gone up into heaven, and taken her, and brought her down from the clouds?* (Baruch 3:29). *And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of Adam which is in heaven.* (John 3:13). Baruch asks a question meant to have no answer: who has gone up into heaven and taken wisdom and brought her down? No one, is the expected reply; wisdom is beyond the reach of any son of Adam. Then Yahusha (Jesus) tells Nicodemus that no man has ascended to heaven except the one who came down from it, the Son of Adam. He is the answer Baruch's question was waiting for. The wisdom no man could climb to fetch came down herself, in flesh; Wisdom of Solomon 9 and Ecclesiasticus 24 had already set her beside the Maker, and John 3:13 names the one who was there and came down.
member_note: Baruch 3:29 — *Who has gone up into heaven, and taken her, and brought her down from the clouds.* The question John 3:13 answers: the Son of Adam came down.

new_note: *Who has gone over the sea, and found her, and will bring her for pure gold?* (Baruch 3:30). *And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of Adam which is in heaven.* (John 3:13). Baruch piles up the impossibility. No one has gone up to heaven to bring wisdom down, and no one has crossed the sea to find her and buy her with pure gold; *No man knoweth her way, nor thinketh of her path* (Baruch 3:31). Yahusha (Jesus) tells Nicodemus that no man has ascended to heaven but the one who came down from it. The reaching Baruch rules out, upward or outward, is answered from the other direction. The Son of Adam did not have to search for wisdom over the sea, because he came down from where she dwells, and he sat in front of Nicodemus as the thing no gold could buy.
member_note: Baruch 3:30 — *Who has gone over the sea, and found her, and will bring her for pure gold.* Wisdom past man's reach; the Son of Adam came down from where she dwells (John 3:13).

new_note: *He has found out all the way of knowledge, and has given it to Jacob his servant, and to Yashar'el (Israel) his beloved.* (Baruch 3:36). *The Son of Adam came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children.* (Matthew 11:19). Baruch says the whole way of knowledge was found out by Elohim (God) and then given, not to the world at large but to Jacob his servant and to Yashar'el (Israel) his beloved. Wisdom has a people she was given to. Yahusha (Jesus), reproached for eating with publicans and sinners, says wisdom is justified of her children: the ones who recognize her are her own. The children of wisdom in Matthew 11 are the covenant seed Baruch names, the people the knowledge was given to, and when the one who gave it stood among them in flesh they knew his voice even when the leaders did not. Her children are the proof she was given to Jacob.
member_note: Baruch 3:36 — *has given it to Jacob his servant, and to Yashar'el (Israel) his beloved.* Wisdom's children at Matthew 11:19 are the people she was given to.

new_note: *Afterward did he shew himself upon earth, and conversed with men.* (Baruch 3:37). *And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of Adam which is in heaven.* (John 3:13). Baruch closes his search for wisdom with a sentence most Bibles no longer carry: afterward he shewed himself upon earth, and conversed with men. The one who alone knows the way of knowledge came down and walked among men. John 3:13 is the same event from the inside; the Son of Adam who came down from heaven is the only one who was ever up there. Baruch said the descent would come; Nicodemus was sitting across from it. The wisdom no man could fetch down from the clouds was in the room, talking with him.
member_note: Baruch 3:37 — *Afterward did he shew himself upon earth, and conversed with men.* The descent John 3:13 names: the Son of Adam who came down from heaven.

new_note: *This is the book of the commandments of Yahuah (God), and the law that endureth for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life; but such as leave it shall die.* (Baruch 4:1). *The Son of Adam came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children.* (Matthew 11:19). Baruch names what the wisdom given to Jacob is: the book of the commandments of Yahuah (God), the law that endures for ever, which gives life to those who keep it and death to those who leave it. Wisdom is not a mood or a philosophy; she is the Torah. So when Yahusha (Jesus) says wisdom is justified of her children, her children are the ones who keep the commandments. John says the same thing from the other side: *He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him* (1 John 2:4). The law that endureth for ever has not been set aside by the one who spoke it at Sinai and walked in Galilee; wisdom's children are known by keeping it.
member_note: Baruch 4:1 — *the law that endureth for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life.* Wisdom is the Torah; her children keep it (Matthew 11:19).

new_note: *This is the book of the commandments of Yahuah (God), and the law that endureth for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life; but such as leave it shall die. Turn you, O Jacob, and take hold of it: walk in the presence of the light thereof, that you may be illuminated.* (Baruch 4:1–2). *But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.* (Deuteronomy 30:14). Baruch sets the book of the commandments before Jacob and says take hold of it, walk in its light. Moses had said the same about the same book: the word is not up in heaven or across the sea, it is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it (Deuteronomy 30:11–14). Both speak of the Torah as a thing within reach, not an impossible standard set up to show failure but a lamp handed to a people to walk by. Baruch's turn you, O Jacob, and take hold of it is Moses's that thou mayest do it, spoken again to the exiles.
member_note: Baruch 4:1 — *This is the book of the commandments of Yahuah (God), and the law that endureth for ever.* Near and keepable, as Deuteronomy 30:14 says of the same word.
flag: Old note's point (take hold of it) sits in v.2, so 4:1-2 are quoted together and cited as Baruch 4:1-2.

new_note: *For my hope is in the Everlasting, that he will save you; and joy is come to me from the Holy One, because of the mercy which shall soon come to you from the Everlasting our Saviour.* (Baruch 4:22). *As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.* (Isaiah 66:13). Jerusalem speaks here as a mother whose children were carried off, and she tells them her hope: the Everlasting will save them, and joy has already come to her from the Holy One because of the mercy soon coming. Isaiah had promised that Yahuah (God) would comfort his people as a mother comforts, and that they would be comforted in Jerusalem. The mother's joy in Baruch and the mother's comfort in Isaiah are one promise, told from the city's side and from the side of Yahuah (God). The comfort is the children coming home; the chapter ends with them gathered from east to west (Baruch 4:37).
member_note: Baruch 4:22 — *joy is come to me from the Holy One, because of the mercy which shall soon come.* The mother's comfort of Isaiah 66:13, told from Jerusalem's side.

new_note: *O Jerusalem, look about you toward the east, and behold the joy that comes to you from Yahuah (God).* (Baruch 4:36). *As he spake to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed for ever.* (Luke 1:55). Jerusalem is told to turn east, the direction her children were carried, and watch the joy coming back to her from Yahuah (God); the next verse says what the joy is, her sons gathered from east to west. Mary ends her song on the ground that joy stands on: Yahuah (God) spoke to the fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever. The gathering is how the oath to Abraham is kept. Baruch's song and Mary's are singing one thing, a seed promised to the fathers, scattered, and now being brought home because he remembers what he said.
member_note: Baruch 4:36 — *look about you toward the east, and behold the joy that comes to you from Yahuah (God).* The gathering that keeps the oath to Abraham and his seed for ever (Luke 1:55).

new_note: *O Jerusalem, look about you toward the east, and behold the joy that comes to you from Yahuah (God).* (Baruch 4:36). *Lift up thine eyes round about, and behold: all these gather themselves together, and come to thee. As I live, saith Yahuah (LORD), thou shalt surely clothe thee with them all, as with an ornament, and bind them on thee, as a bride doeth.* (Isaiah 49:18). Baruch tells Jerusalem to look east and behold the joy coming to her; Isaiah tells her to lift up her eyes round about and behold her children gathering and coming to her, so many she will wear them like a bride's ornaments. The same city is told to look up in both, and what she sees is the same: her own children coming back. Isaiah swears it by the life of Yahuah (LORD). Baruch, writing from the captivity, is holding Isaiah's promise up for the exiles to see.
member_note: Baruch 4:36 — *behold the joy that comes to you from Yahuah (God).* Isaiah's lift up thine eyes upon the gathering children (Isaiah 49:18).

new_note: *Lo, your sons come, whom you sentest away, they come gathered together from the east to the west by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the glory of Yahuah (God).* (Baruch 4:37). *As he spake to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed for ever.* (Luke 1:55). Here is what Jerusalem sees when she looks east: her sons, the ones she sent away, coming gathered from east to west by the word of the Holy One. Mary's song ends with the seed those sons belong to; Yahuah (God) spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever. The sons gathered in Baruch are Abraham's seed, scattered by exile and brought back because the oath was for ever. The Magnificat names the promise; Baruch names its fulfillment walking home.
member_note: Baruch 4:37 — *your sons come, whom you sentest away, they come gathered together from the east to the west.* Abraham's seed for ever, gathered home (Luke 1:55).

new_note: *Lo, your sons come, whom you sentest away, they come gathered together from the east to the west by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the glory of Yahuah (God).* (Baruch 4:37). *And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of Elohim (God) that were scattered abroad.* (John 11:52). Baruch sees the sons Jerusalem sent away coming gathered from east to west by the word of the Holy One. John explains the death of Yahusha (Jesus) in the same terms: not for that nation only, but to gather into one the children of Elohim (God) that were scattered abroad. The scattered children are not the nations; they are Jerusalem's own sons, sent away in the scattering, the ones Hosea said would be called sons of the living Elohim (God) in the very place they were called not his people (Hosea 1:10). Baruch names the gathering by the word of the Holy One; John names the death that does the gathering.
member_note: Baruch 4:37 — *they come gathered together from the east to the west by the word of the Holy One.* The scattered children of Elohim (God) gathered into one (John 11:52).

new_note: *Arise, O Jerusalem, and stand on high, and look about toward the east, and behold your children gathered from the west to the east by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the remembrance of Yahuah (God).* (Baruch 5:5). *And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven.* (Mark 13:27). Baruch 4:37 brought the children from east to west; here they come from west to east. Between the two verses the gathering comes from every direction. Mark 13:27 says it the same way: the Son of Adam sends his angels to gather his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth. Jerusalem's children in Baruch and the elect in Mark are one people, the scattered seed, brought home by the word of the Holy One and the hand of the Son of Adam at the end of the age. Jerusalem is told to stand on high and watch, because the homecoming is something she will see.
member_note: Baruch 5:5 — *behold your children gathered from the west to the east by the word of the Holy One.* With 4:37 the gathering comes from every direction; the elect from the four winds (Mark 13:27).

new_note: *Arise, O Jerusalem, and stand on high, and look about toward the east, and behold your children gathered from the west to the east by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the remembrance of Yahuah (God). For they departed from you on foot, and were led away of their enemies: but Yahuah (God) brings them to you exalted with glory, as children of the kingdom.* (Baruch 5:5–6). *And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of Elohim (God).* (Luke 13:29). Jerusalem is told to stand up high and watch her children come home from the west to the east, and the next verse says who they are: the ones who left her on foot, led away by their enemies, now brought back by Yahuah (God) exalted with glory as children of the kingdom. Yahusha (Jesus) says they shall come from the east and the west and the north and the south and sit down in the kingdom of Elohim (God). The ones who come from every quarter in Luke 13 are the same children of the kingdom Baruch watches return, not strangers streaming in, but Jerusalem's own sons who were led away and are being brought home.
member_note: Baruch 5:5 — *Arise, O Jerusalem, and stand on high, and look about toward the east.* Jerusalem's own children brought home as children of the kingdom; they come from east and west to sit down in it (Luke 13:29).
flag: Old note leaned on 5:6 (children of the kingdom) for its point, so 5:5-6 are quoted together and cited as Baruch 5:5-6; no move, 5:5 is still the card's verse.

new_note: *Arise, O Jerusalem, and stand on high, and look about toward the east, and behold your children gathered from the west to the east by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the remembrance of Yahuah (God).* (Baruch 5:5). *And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of Elohim (God) that were scattered abroad.* (John 11:52). Baruch says it twice, once in chapter 4 and again here, so no one misses it: Jerusalem's children are gathered by the word of the Holy One, from the east and from the west. John says the death of Yahusha (Jesus) was to gather together in one the children of Elohim (God) that were scattered abroad. Scattered abroad is where Baruch's children went; gathered into one is where they are going. The homecoming Baruch sang from the captivity is the homecoming John says the cross was for.
member_note: Baruch 5:5 — *your children gathered from the west to the east by the word of the Holy One.* The scattered children gathered into one (John 11:52).

new_note: *For Yahuah (God) has appointed that every high hill, and banks of long continuance, should be cast down, and valleys filled up, to make even the ground, that Yashar'el (Israel) may go safely in the glory of Yahuah (God),* (Baruch 5:7). *Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth;* (Luke 3:5). Baruch gives the reason the hills come down and the valleys fill: so that Yashar'el (Israel) may walk home safely in the glory of Yahuah (God). The leveled road is a road for the gathering. John the Baptist preached from Isaiah 40, every valley filled, every mountain brought low, the rough ways made smooth, and Luke tells us who was walking that road: the people coming out to him to be baptized, the house of Yashar'el (Israel) being called back. Baruch read Isaiah's highway as the road the scattered seed comes home on; John stood at the head of that road and opened it.
member_note: Baruch 5:7 — *every high hill, and banks of long continuance, should be cast down, and valleys filled up.* The leveled road is for Yashar'el (Israel) to walk home; John opened it (Luke 3:5).

new_note: *For Yahuah (God) shall lead Yashar'el (Israel) with joy in the light of his glory with the mercy and righteousness that comes from him.* (Baruch 5:9). *And all flesh shall see the salvation of Elohim (God).* (Luke 3:6). Baruch ends his gathering song with Yahuah (God) himself leading Yashar'el (Israel) home with joy, in the light of his glory, in mercy and righteousness. Luke ends his quotation of Isaiah 40 with all flesh seeing the salvation of Elohim (God). The two endings belong together: the road is leveled so Yashar'el (Israel) can walk it, and when Yahuah (God) leads them home in his glory the whole earth watches. The salvation all flesh sees is the gathering of the scattered seed; the nations see it done, and Yashar'el (Israel) walks it.
member_note: Baruch 5:9 — *Yahuah (God) shall lead Yashar'el (Israel) with joy in the light of his glory.* Where the road ends; all flesh sees the salvation of Elohim (God) (Luke 3:6).

new_note: *For Yahuah (God) shall lead Yashar'el (Israel) with joy in the light of his glory with the mercy and righteousness that comes from him.* (Baruch 5:9). *And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of Elohim (God) that were scattered abroad.* (John 11:52). Baruch's song ends with the gathering complete: Yahuah (God) leads Yashar'el (Israel) home with joy in the light of his glory. John names what the death of Yahusha (Jesus) accomplished in the same terms, gathering into one the children of Elohim (God) that were scattered abroad. The scattered children and Yashar'el (Israel) led home are one people; John's into one is Baruch's led with joy. The mercy and righteousness that come from him in Baruch came in the flesh in John, and the gathering they promised runs through the cross.
member_note: Baruch 5:9 — *with the mercy and righteousness that comes from him.* Yashar'el (Israel) led home with joy is the scattered children gathered into one (John 11:52).
